blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Structure-from-motion (SfM) from the dual-fisheye video of a consumer 360-degree camera recovers geometry only up to a similarity transform; in the pipeline considered here, metric scale is obtained from smartphone ARKit or ARCore poses captured alongside the camera. This paper evaluates a self-contained alternative: the IMU embedded in the Insta360 X5 and X6, recorded at 1 kHz. The sensor is characterised (noise density, camera-IMU synchronisation, accelerometer scale factor, bias stability), the camera-IMU rotation and frame timing are estimated from the data, and the scale is recovered by a linear visual-inertial alignment over the SfM poses of a whole survey. The standard formulation, with gravity and accelerometer bias shared across the survey, overestimates the scale by 3.4% on average; estimating each contiguous segment independently and averaging removes the bias. On nine surveys with a co-mounted LiDAR scanner the inertial scale deviates from the LiDAR by 0.74% in mean absolute error, against 1.94% for the smartphone scale; on printed fiducial markers both agree within the 1% uncertainty of the target. On the reference trajectories of thirty sequences of a public benchmark, brought to scales of 1/40, 1 and 40, the estimator recovers the metric scale with a mean error of -0.07% and a standard deviation of 1.28%. On fifty production surveys where the smartphone is the only reference, the two scales agree to a standard deviation of 2.6%, the inertial scale being 0.9% lower on average; the difference does not depend on window construction, grows with the extent of the smartphone anchor, and cannot be attributed to either reference. An ablation over window construction and a comparison with monocular metric-depth networks complete the study.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Structure-from-motion without a baseline of known length recovers scene
structure and camera trajectory up to a similarity transform: shape and
trajectory are determined, absolute size is not. For a mapping pipeline
that reconstructs scenes from the native dual-fisheye video of an
Insta360 camera, the missing scale must be supplied by an external
measurement. The current solution uses a smartphone carried by the
operator. During the survey the operator captures a burst of photographs
whose poses are metric, from ARKit on iOS or ARCore on Android; the
photographs are registered jointly with the fisheye frames, and a robust
alignment transfers the smartphone scale to the model.

blocks.en:
This arrangement has three costs. It requires a second device and a
second capture procedure. It makes the metric reference heterogeneous,
since the two smartphone platforms and their versions behave
differently. And it extrapolates from a small spatial baseline: the
burst is taken within about 15 s over a few metres, so the metric scale
of a survey of several hundred metres rests on a short segment of it,
and any error in the smartphone poses over that segment propagates to
the whole model. Section 5.2 quantifies the consequence: across nine
surveys with a co-mounted LiDAR scanner, the smartphone-anchored models
deviate from the LiDAR by 1.9% in mean absolute error, with individual
surveys reaching 4.4%. The smartphone remains a serviceable reference,
and this figure is its measured accuracy rather than a failure; the
question addressed here is whether a sensor already inside the camera
can take its place.

blocks.en:
The Insta360 X5 and X6 contain a gyroscope and an accelerometer sampled
at 1000 Hz and written into the recording. The accelerometer measures
specific force in metres per second squared. For a trajectory expressed
in the arbitrary units of an SfM model there is exactly one scale factor
for which its second derivative agrees with the measured accelerations
once gravity is accounted for. Recovering that factor is the
visual-inertial initialisation problem, which is well studied in the
context of real-time SLAM [ 16 , 17 , 21 ] . The setting here differs
in three respects: the poses are the output of an offline SfM pipeline
rather than a tracker, the alignment is performed in batch over surveys
lasting minutes rather than over the first seconds of motion, and the
frames used by the reconstruction are sparse in time, several per second
at most, while the IMU is continuous.

blocks.en: The contributions of this paper are the following.
blocks.zh: 本文件的贡献如下。

blocks.en:
1. A characterisation of the embedded IMU of the Insta360 X5 and X6 as
recorded in the .insv container: noise density, camera-IMU time offset
and axis mapping, accelerometer scale factor and bias stability. 2. A data-driven estimation of the camera-IMU rotation and of the affine
frame-timing model, together with a diagnostic that detects a wrong
timing model without ground truth. 3. Evidence that the joint linear alignment over a whole survey, with
shared gravity and accelerometer bias, is biased high by 3.4% on the
surveys with external reference, and that a segment-wise estimate
followed by averaging removes the bias. An ablation over window
construction shows that the improvement is due to not sharing the
nuisance parameters and is insensitive to how the survey is divided. 4. An evaluation against four independent references: nine surveys with a
co-mounted LiDAR scanner, one survey with printed fiducial markers of
known geometry, 62 production surveys with smartphone poses, and the
reference trajectories of thirty sequences of a public benchmark. On
the LiDAR surveys the inertial scale is 2.4 times more accurate than
the smartphone reference. 5. A comparison with monocular metric-depth networks as an alternative
scale source, showing that their scene-dependent bias makes them
unsuitable as a reference at the accuracy level considered.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Visual-inertial initialisation. The linear relation between
camera displacement, velocity, gravity and preintegrated accelerometer
measurements was formulated in closed form by Martinelli [ 16 ] and
is used to bootstrap visual-inertial SLAM systems, including ORB-SLAM
with inertial support [ 17 ] and VINS-Mono [ 21 ] . Campos et
al. [ 4 ] refine the linear solution by an inertial-only
maximum-a-posteriori optimisation. Preintegration of the inertial
measurements between camera frames follows Lupton and Sukkarieh [ 15 ] , placed on the manifold by Forster et al. [ 8 ] . These
systems initialise over a few seconds of motion and then track online.
The present work applies the same linear formulation offline, in batch
over a whole survey, to poses produced by an SfM pipeline; the
differences that arise at that time scale, in particular the behaviour
of the shared gravity and bias parameters, are the subject of Section
5.6 and Section 6.1.

floating-point values that the firmware has low-pass filtered. Files
exported by the manufacturer’s desktop software lose the metadata.

blocks.en: 3.6 Quality criteria
blocks.zh: 3.6 质量标准

blocks.en:
Several quantities are computed to make the estimate verifiable, all of
them from the per-run solutions rather than from the joint one. Gravity
is left unconstrained in every run: its magnitude is not needed for the
scale, but a correct alignment must recover it, and a run whose gravity
magnitude falls outside 9.3 to 10.3 m s -2 indicates a wrong timing
model, a wrong camera-IMU rotation or a defective reconstruction and is
discarded; a survey in which such runs hold more than half of the
intervals is reported as failed. The gravity direction used to level the
model is the interval-weighted mean of the per-run gravity vectors. The
dispersion of the per-run scales is reported with the estimate; its
standard deviation across runs is 1 to 3% on the surveys of Section 5,
so the standard error of the mean over five to thirteen runs is 0.3 to
1.5%. A survey whose standard error exceeds 2.5%, or which yields
fewer than four usable runs, is reported as failed. The per-run scales
of the first and second half of the trajectory are averaged separately;
a disagreement above 6% indicates internal scale drift in the model,
and the per-run values identify segments where the scale is weakly
observable, which occurs when the operator moves at constant velocity
and the accelerometer measures little beyond gravity. The joint solution
and its bootstrap dispersion are still computed and reported as
diagnostics, since a large gap between the joint solution and the
per-run mean indicates that gravity or bias is not constant over the
survey, but they do not enter the acceptance decision. Intervals whose
residual exceeds five times the median are removed before a second
solve. The second solve isolates segments in which the SfM itself is
misregistered: on one survey with 19 m discontinuities in the trajectory
the estimator does not converge after outlier removal and reports
failure rather than a scale.

blocks.en:
All poses used in this study are taken unchanged from the production
reconstruction pipeline: COLMAP-format models built from the native
dual-fisheye frames with learned features, retrieval-based matching and
a two-lens rig constraint in bundle adjustment, that is, the standard
components of current large-scale SfM. No reconstruction was recomputed
for this work. The estimator reads the frames of one lens of the rig;
lens 1 is used on every survey, a choice fixed before any result was
read, and lens 0 is reported as a robustness check. All results are
computed with the public implementation of the estimator at its default
settings [ 18 ] . Each registered frame carries its video frame
index, so frame times follow from it, and frames discarded by the
sharpness filter leave gaps without renumbering.

blocks.en: 4.2 Reference measurements

blocks.en:
LiDAR. The scanner builds its map with LiDAR SLAM of the LOAM
family. For each survey the LiDAR cloud and the pipeline reconstruction
were aligned by a closed-form trajectory initialisation followed by a
scaled iterative-closest-point cascade on the dense clouds, which
returns the factor converting the reconstruction into LiDAR metres.
Since the reconstruction is anchored to the smartphone, that factor is
also the error of the smartphone reference. The scanner’s specified
accuracy is 2 cm at 10 m, 3 cm at 20 m and 5 cm at 40 m. This is a
per-point figure and does not limit a scale comparison: the factor is
recovered from millions of points along a whole trajectory, so the
random part averages out, while the systematic part of a time-of-flight
range is set by a crystal oscillator. The LiDAR map may drift in shape
over long paths, but every distance within it is measured in metres
directly, which is the quantity the reconstruction lacks.

blocks.en: 5.1 Sensor characterisation
blocks.zh: 5.1 传感器特性化

blocks.en:
Noise density. No static recording was available at the outset,
and a moving recording contains the operator’s motion superimposed on
sensor noise. The two are separable in frequency: walking and hand
motion occupy the band below 50 Hz, so the band from 100 Hz to the
Nyquist frequency of 500 Hz contains sensor noise only. The amplitude
spectral density of the gyroscope was estimated with Welch’s method over
80 s of hand-held recording (Figure 1). The X6 spectrum is flat above
100 Hz at about 0.006 degrees per second per square root hertz, white
noise at the level of a good consumer MEMS device. The X5 spectrum
continues to fall with frequency, identifying the firmware low-pass
filter. The accelerometer shows an internal low-pass filter as well,
with an upper bound of 1 to 5 mm s -2 Hz -1/2 on its noise
density. The sensor noise is therefore compatible with visual-inertial
alignment, and the X5 values are filtered rather than raw.

blocks.en:
Synchronisation and axis mapping. Integrating the accelerometer
over a frame interval presumes that frame timestamps and IMU timestamps
refer to the same clock; a residual offset would shift every integration
window and bias the scale. To test this without a calibration target,
the camera rotation was estimated from the video alone and compared with
the gyroscope. Shi-Tomasi corners [ 25 ] were tracked between
consecutive frames with pyramidal Lucas-Kanade optical flow [ 3 ] and a forward-backward consistency check; the tracks were unprojected
with an equidistant fisheye model, and the inter-frame rotation was
estimated by Kabsch alignment inside a RANSAC loop [ 7 ] under a
pure-rotation assumption. The resulting angular rate was compared with
the gyroscope rate averaged over the same frame interval, for gyroscope
time shifts from − - 150 to +150 ms in 1 ms steps and for all signed
permutations of the three axes, retaining the combination with the
highest mean absolute correlation. On a hand-held sequence with angular
rates up to 480 degrees per second the mean correlation is 0.993 and the
maximum lies at − - 2 ms (Figure 2): the IMU timestamps in the file
already refer to the video clock. The correlation curve is broad because
each visual sample averages the rotation over a 42 ms frame interval, so
the offset is bounded to about ±5 ms rather than resolved to the
millisecond. The axis mapping is identical across firmware versions
1.0.6 and 1.11.6, and the rear lens is related to the front lens by a
180-degree rotation about the vertical image axis.

blocks.en:
Accelerometer scale factor and bias stability. Two properties
of the accelerometer bear directly on the scale: whether its scale
factor is correct, and how far its zero moves during a survey. Both were
obtained from an eleven-minute recording with the camera resting on a
table. The gyroscope confirms that the camera is stationary, with the
norm of the angular rate below 0.44 degrees per second at the 99th
percentile. The mean magnitude of the measured specific force is 9.8092
m s -2 , against a local gravity of 9.806 m s -2 at the
latitude of the recording; the accelerometer scale factor is therefore
correct to 0.03%, which excludes a sensor gain error as an explanation
for any scale discrepancy. The bias drifts monotonically with the shape
of a thermal warm-up, fastest in the first five minutes and flattening
afterwards. Averaged in ten-second blocks, the x axis moves from − - 0.376 to − - 0.408 m s -2 and the z axis from − - 0.108 to − - 0.132 m s -2 , a vector excursion of 0.042 m s -2 over ten
and a half minutes; on a survey of three minutes the expected excursion
is about 0.013 m s -2 . This is an order of magnitude below the
value that would be required to explain the bias of the joint
formulation (Section 6.1). The gyroscope bias over the same recording
has a magnitude of 0.18 degrees per second with an excursion of 0.30
degrees per second, which amounts to 0.06 degrees over one frame
interval and is negligible for the hand-eye estimate. The recording is
from a third X5 unit, not one of the two used in the surveys; it
establishes the order of magnitude of both effects rather than the exact
figures for those units.

blocks.en:
Table 2 reports the scale error of the inertial estimate and of the
smartphone reference relative to the LiDAR on the nine surveys; a
positive error denotes a scale larger than the LiDAR. The inertial scale
has a mean error of +0.07%, a mean absolute error of 0.81% and a worst
case of 2.11%. The smartphone reference has a mean error of − - 0.41%,
a mean absolute error of 1.94% and a worst case of 4.36%. Neither
reference shows a systematic sign, as expected of two unbiased
references, but the inertial scale is the closer of the two on seven of
the nine surveys and is more accurate by a factor of 2.4 overall (Figure
4). The smartphone column mixes ARKit and ARCore, which is
representative of the fleet and is one of the costs noted in Section 1.
The dispersion of the per-run inertial estimates within each survey is
1.1% to 3.2%, giving a standard error of the mean between 0.5% and
1.4%, consistent with the scatter observed against the LiDAR.

blocks.en:
The marker reference itself carries a 1% uncertainty. Marker sides
measured in model units imply a scale of 1.011 to 1.021, whereas centre
distances imply 0.997 to 0.998; the discrepancy is systematic on both
sheets and corresponds to an inward bias of the corner localisation of
1.5% to 2% at a marker size of about 130 pixels, so the centre-based
estimate is preferred. Rectifying the sheet through the marker
homography shows a paper width of 300 to 301 mm against the A3 nominal
of 297 mm, that is, the printed content is about 1% smaller than the
layout. After this correction the marker-derived scale lies between
0.987 and 1.005. The inertial estimate on this survey is 0.989 and the
ARKit scale is 1.000; both fall inside the marker interval (Figure 5).

blocks.en:
All twelve surveys were processed with the same settings and without
manual intervention. The ratio between the inertial scale and the ARKit
scale has a mean of 0.991, a median of 0.994 and a standard deviation of
3.0%, with extremes of 0.947 and 1.035 (Figure 6, left). The lowest
ratio belongs to the reprocessed indoor recording (A12), in which the
smartphone photographs cover an area of only 2 by 1.4 m; a monocular
depth estimate on the same model agrees with the inertial scale (0.956
against ARKit). The internal uncertainty of the inertial estimate, a
median disagreement of 1.5% between trajectory halves, accounts for
part of the dispersion; the remainder is attributable to the ARKit
reference, in line with the 2.9% error of that reference on LiDAR
survey L1. No systematic offset between the two references is resolved
on this sample; Section 5.5 examines the offset on a larger one. The
recovered gravity magnitude is 9.77 ± 0.08 m s -2 across
the surveys.

blocks.en:
This section separates the two decisions involved in the segment-wise
estimate, how the survey is divided into windows and how the window
estimates are combined, and measures each against the ten surveys with
external ground truth (the nine LiDAR surveys and the fiducial survey).
Three window constructions were compared. Contiguous runs uses
the natural segmentation, in which a run ends wherever the pipeline has
discarded frames. Fixed windows cuts each run into consecutive
blocks of N N intervals. Sliding windows takes every window of N N intervals at stride one, so that windows overlap and each interval
is counted many times. A stride variant interpolates between the last
two, taking windows of 30 intervals at a stride of 15. Every variant
estimates each window independently and reports the mean.

windowed variant improves on the single joint system by a factor between

The scale of the input model is unknown by assumption and its
orientation is arbitrary. Gross per-run outliers are therefore rejected
relative to the median of the per-run scales, never against an absolute
range, and the joint solution is not used as a reference because it can
fail on its own (Section 6.1). To confirm that the estimator exploits
neither the scale nor the orientation of the input, each of the thirty
reference trajectories of the public benchmark (Section 5.8) was
transformed by a similarity with a scale factor of 1/40, 1 and 40, a
random rotation and a random translation, and supplied to the estimator.
On every sequence the three recovered scales are identical once divided
by the applied factor, to within the printed precision of 0.0001%, and
every run passes the quality criteria. The input model may therefore be
supplied in any units and any orientation.

Outdoor surveys are worse on average, with a mean absolute bias of 11%

split is not clean: two indoor surveys (A1, A3) are recovered within 1%

6.1 Bias of the joint
formulation

The largest single effect in the method is the choice between a joint
solution with shared nuisance parameters and a segment-wise solution.
Against external ground truth the joint solution is biased high by
3.39% with consistent sign (Table 3), and on the fifty surveys of set B
it lies above the segment-wise mean on 34 and fails on three. On the
reference trajectories of the public benchmark, which carry no
reconstruction error, the joint solution is unbiased ( − - 0.06% on
average), which places the source of the bias in the reconstructions
rather than in the sensor. The static recording of Section 5.1 bounds
the accelerometer bias drift at 0.042 m s -2 over ten minutes, an
order of magnitude below what would be required to produce the observed
shift through the bias term alone, so bias drift is excluded as the
cause. The remaining candidate is the gravity term. If the effective
gravity direction in the model frame is not constant along the survey,
for instance because of residual orientation drift in the

blocks.en:
6.2 Offset on the production sample and the absence of ground
truth
blocks.zh:
6.2 生产样品的偏移和没有地面
事实

blocks.en:
On fifty production surveys the inertial scale lies 0.3% below the
smartphone scale on average, on 31 of the fifty. The difference is not
correlated with run length, survey duration or path length, and it is of
the same size as the difference between the two lenses of the rig
(0.6%). It does vary with the spatial extent of the smartphone anchor:
on the 42 surveys anchored over less than 12 m the inertial scale is
0.8% lower, while on the eight anchored over 16 to 29 m it is 2.4%
higher. The difference between the two references is therefore not a
constant property of either, and on average it is smaller than the error
the smartphone reference carries against LiDAR, so the two references
are not in contradiction. The point to retain is that on production
surveys no ground truth exists: the smartphone scale is itself an
estimate with a measured error of 1.9% and a worst case of 4.4%, and
an agreement of 2.3% between two independent estimates of that quality
is what one expects when both are approximately right. Taken together,
the LiDAR, fiducial and smartphone comparisons bound the error of the
inertial scale at below 1% in mean absolute error, 2.1% in the worst
case, where an instrument reading metres is available and at 3 to 4% in
the worst case against the smartphone, with no configuration in which
the inertial estimate disagrees with every other reference. The source
of the residual difference on set B, and of its dependence on the
anchor, can only be assigned by a third, metric measurement on the same
scenes, which is left to future work.

blocks.en: 6.3 Quality criteria
blocks.zh: 6.3 质量标准

blocks.en:
The quality criteria were originally designed for the joint estimator,
and three of them, the recovered gravity magnitude, the bootstrap
dispersion and the half-versus-half comparison, were read from the joint
solution. On an earlier sample of fifty production surveys that version
rejected six whose segment-wise estimates are unremarkable, and on the
LiDAR set it rejected one survey whose scale is accurate to 0.39%; in
every such case the joint solution had either collapsed or recovered a
gravity magnitude far from 9.81 m s -2 while the per-run solutions
were normal. The criteria were therefore restated on the per-run
quantities, as described in Section 3.6: gravity is checked run by run,
the two halves are compared as means of per-run scales, and the
bootstrap of the joint solution is retained only as a diagnostic. Under
this version all fifty surveys of set B pass, and the drift of the time
offset along the survey (Section 3.3), the hand-eye residual and the
dispersion of the per-run scales remain the criteria that reject a
defective alignment.

blocks.en: 6.4 Limitations
blocks.zh: 6.4 限制

blocks.en:
The LiDAR reference is a consumer SLAM instrument whose drift over long
paths has not been characterised independently; its per-point accuracy
does not limit a scale comparison drawn from millions of points, and it
agrees with the smartphone reference to within 1% on average with no
systematic sign, but a tape measurement of a known object on one of the
LiDAR sites remains the only way to validate either reference without
assuming the other. The results of Section 5.4 were computed with the
joint estimator and could not be recomputed on all twelve models. The
estimator reads one lens of the rig; the two lenses give similar
accuracy against the LiDAR but differ by 0.6% on average on the
production surveys, for a reason not isolated here. All surveys with
external reference were recorded with the X5, while the X6 is
characterised as a sensor only. The static characterisation was
performed on a third camera unit and establishes orders of magnitude
rather than unit-specific figures; a longer static recording would allow
a proper Allan-variance analysis of bias instability. Finally, the
linear alignment is not followed by a non-linear refinement with
preintegration factors and gyroscope bias, which the visual-inertial
SLAM literature uses to improve on the closed-form initialisation.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
The IMU embedded in the Insta360 X5 and X6, combined with the camera
poses that the SfM pipeline already computes, yields a metric scale
without smartphone data. The sensor is recorded at 1 kHz on the video
clock to within ±5 ms, its accelerometer scale factor is correct
to 0.03% and its bias moves by 0.042 m s -2 over ten minutes. A
linear visual-inertial alignment recovers the scale of existing
reconstructions, independently of the units and orientation of the input
model, provided that the frame timing is estimated from the data rather
than taken at its nominal value and that the alignment is solved per
contiguous segment rather than jointly over the survey. The segment-wise
estimate reduces the mean absolute error against external reference from
3.43% to 0.85%. On nine surveys with a co-mounted LiDAR the inertial
scale deviates by 0.81% in mean absolute error against 1.94% for the
smartphone reference, and on printed fiducial markers both references
fall within the 1% uncertainty of the target. On the reference
trajectories of thirty sequences of a public benchmark the estimator is
unbiased, with a mean error of − - 0.07% and a dispersion of 1.28% per
sequence, whatever the scale of the input. On fifty production surveys
the two references agree to a standard deviation of 2.3%, with an
unattributed mean difference of 0.3% that varies with the extent of the
smartphone anchor and, by a similar amount, with the lens of the rig
used for the estimate. The smartphone capture step can therefore be
removed from the procedure, with the recovered gravity magnitude, the
drift of the video-to-IMU offset and the dispersion of the per-run
scales available to reject a failed alignment. Open items are a third
metric reference on the production sample, which is the only way to
assign the residual difference to one of the two estimates, and a
non-linear refinement of the linear solution.
